remaining_scientific_objections.objection: The local girls/boys contrast is real, but the later author conclusion says the study largely replicated the findings, particularly theory–practice and gender gaps. The claimed absence of a governing broad verdict needs scientific resolution.

Abstract reports age-driven mortality prediction and construct critique; it does not explicitly say the original mortality/criterion associations replicated as claimed. New MIDUS associations cannot alone establish full original replication.

The main author synthesis affirms verbal overshadowing in both large replications. The contrasting secondary error-type distribution is real but the existing reason assumes it overrides that whole-target conclusion; scientific scope review is required.

Authors apply preregistered criteria and call temporal effect direction consistent but magnitude inconsistent, in an overall limited-support synthesis. Treating this solely as smaller-but-successful suppresses their stated replication qualification.

Appendix says the same sources were accessed but original sample could not be matched: 2054 rather than 1993 cumulative years because newer TFR data were included. Existing exact-original-data rationale overstates sample identity.

Abstract distinguishes nonsignificant Spanish independent sample from supportive pooled meta-analysis including previous data. The broad gene-risk conclusion is not an unqualified verdict on the independent retest.

Discussion reports inferior performance and code/method discrepancies, but under adapted Colab execution and reduced training/resolution. This does not establish failure of identical original computation; existing reason must preserve this non-equivalence when assigning computation issues.

Author says search costs may explain overbidding and rejection of standard model is premature; existing reason overstates this as demonstration that search costs explain it. Raw text even contains an apparent missing negation; no OCR/sign repair is permissible.

Discussion explicitly says similar to Smaby and compares MSA viability, then compares suitability with Cividini-Motta/Ahearn. Existing reason says only general viability rather than an empirical comparison; descriptive-only scope needs resolution.

Paper explicitly targets Hulstijn partial conceptual replication, but abstract also evaluates Segalowitz hypothesis and says no counterevidence. Treating Segalowitz as exclusively methodological background overstates the primary text; original empirical retest versus theoretical validation needs resolution.

Thesis abstract establishes Sonbul/Schmitt retest but cannot establish equality of two repository DOI records, source downloads and shipped rows. Existing duplicate-removal rationale relies on external provenance rather than this primary passage.

Authors replicate under successive-gains criterion but immediately say statistical analysis failed for A, procedure needs refinement, and group design demands statistically significant differences. Existing reason understates this methodological qualification.

Authors call direct results very close and attribute minor differences to alternative dataset construction. This supports nonidentity, but not failure to rerun identical original observations; computation-axis interpretation must retain reconstructed sample limitation.

Report explicitly says all seven significant effects replicated and four newly significant effects had size/direction consistent with original trends, likely power differences. Existing reason treats this solely as contradictory findings and suppresses their concordance interpretation.

Introduction attributes the Western pass-rate benchmark to Nielsen, Dissanayake and Kashima 2003, but the inspected Methods sticker-procedure citation is Nielsen and Dissanayake 2003 (two authors), alongside Nielsen et al. 2006. Existing reason conflates these identities when claiming method corroboration. Benchmark attribution remains present; original-specific empirical target status needs resolution.

Passage establishes Kim 2006 and Kim/White retest but concerns control-group summer loss, not an overall failed treatment-effect verdict. Heterogeneous effects by school poverty require outcome scope review.
Discussion explicitly compares MSA suitability with Cividini-Motta/Ahearn, not merely task adoption. Descriptive-only outcome rationale needs to account for author empirical comparison.

old_evidence.reason: In the original study (Sabourin et al., 2008), cognitive and affective reactions to running decreased in high AS but not low AS women, whereas somatic reactions decreased in both high and low AS women (Introduction, lines 220-225). While the cognitive and affective decreases (high AS only) and the high-AS somatic decrease replicated, the low-AS somatic decrease did not replicate, which the Discussion explicitly notes was contrary to predictions (lines 709-721). Because some tested findings from the original study replicated and one did not, the outcome is mixed.

issues.contextual_rationale: Discussion names the Sabourin retest and reports agreement for cognitive/affective reactions alongside absent low-AS somatic decline; low group size and floor effects qualify inference.

old_evidence.quote: We generally confirm H&Q's finding of a high CEO effect, but find a smaller industry effect and a larger firm effect in our much larger sample.
old_evidence.location: Abstract, p. 1111 (also Section 5.1, p. 1123; Section 7 Conclusion, p. 1134)
old_evidence.reason: Under the codebook, confirming one specific tested effect is a single comparison rather than an unqualified overall verdict on the replication as a whole, and a tested finding that the paper itself contrasts with the original cannot be left out of the verdict. Throughout the paper (Abstract, Introduction, Section 5.1, Discussion, and Conclusion), the authors compare all variance components of Hambrick and Quigley's (2014) CEO-in-Context (CiC) model in their extended samples against the original results, explicitly contrasting their findings of a much smaller industry effect (0.37% vs. 6.9%) and a larger firm effect (18.65% vs. 12.1%) with their confirmation of a high CEO effect (and further noting that using adjusted R2s markedly reduces the CEO effect). Because the authors explicitly frame their replication results as agreeing on the high CEO effect while differing on the industry and firm effects, the outcome is 'mixed'.

issues.contextual_rationale: Conclusion confirms high CEO effect while contrasting industry and firm effects; use conclusion to avoid abstract sidebar intrusion.

old_evidence.quote: One main finding of this paper is that, while we were unable to detect as strong a primacy effect as Asch (1946) originally reported, on balance there is evidence for a primacy effect in impression formation.
old_evidence.location: General Discussion, lines 1247-1251 (see also Abstract, lines 48-56, and General Discussion, lines 1386-1388)
old_evidence.reason: The paper aimed both to replicate Asch's (1946, Exp. VI) primacy effect in impression formation and to test a novel extension regarding a pragmatic explanation (human vs. random computer speaker). Under the codebook (Step 3, Rule 1 and Coding Rules), where a paper reports multiple studies testing the original finding, they are aggregated following the author's explicit overall verdict, and a smaller effect size than the original still codes as 'successful' when the author treats the finding as supported on balance. The author explicitly concludes that 'on balance there is evidence for a primacy effect in impression formation' and 'In conclusion, we found evidence of a primacy effect in impression formation, although one that is substantially smaller than originally reported by Asch (1946).' The shipped 'mixed' coding improperly conflated the successful replication of Asch's primacy effect with the null result for the novel pragmatic-account extension.

issues.contextual_rationale: General Discussion gives on-balance evidence for primacy despite smaller effects and failures with custom materials; success claim is bounded to original primacy effect.

old_evidence.reason: The replication re-tested both the primary identification accuracy effect (verbal overshadowing) and the original paper's secondary analysis comparing error types (false identifications vs. responding 'not present') across conditions. While the primary verbal overshadowing effect was replicated in both RRR1 and RRR2, the authors explicitly contrast their error-type result with the original finding: whereas Schooler and Engstler-Schooler (1990) reported no difference across conditions in the proportion of errors that were false identifications, both replication studies found a robust difference. Under the codebook rules, finding an effect where the original found none is a disagreement, and where the paper confirms the primary tested effect but explicitly marks another tested finding from the original as differing in its own words ('Although S&E S reported no difference... both replication studies found a robust difference'), the outcome is 'mixed'.

issues.contextual_rationale: The main author synthesis affirms verbal overshadowing in both large replications. The contrasting secondary error-type distribution is real but the existing reason assumes it overrides that whole-target conclusion; scientific scope review is required.

The increase in the initial study can therefore not be linked easily to the media coverage', lines 506-518); and (3) the authors summarize the replication in their final paragraph as having 'helped to solidify some results from the original study' (line 553). Under the codebook, because the authors present their evidence as confirming some original findings while explicitly contrasting others, the outcome is 'mixed'.

By 18 months, approximately 50% pass and by 24 months a significant majority of children (more than 70%) are reported to self- refer by touching or removing a mark from their own body (face or other body region) while exploring their mirror image (Amsterdam, 1972; Asendorpf, Warkentin, & Baudonnière, 1996; Bard, Todd, Bernier, Love, & Leavens, 2006; Bertenthal & Fisher, 1978; Lewis & Brooks-Gunn, 1979; Lewis & Ramsay, 2004; Nielsen, Dissanayake, & Kashima, 2003; Schulman & Kaplowitz, 1976). Here we report cross-cultural observations on the emergence of mirror self-recognition (MSR), using a simplified mark test, raising questions regarding the meaning and universal validity of this test as an ontogenetic benchmark of self-concept.
old_evidence.reason: Nielsen, Dissanayake, and Kashima (2003) is both attributed in the introduction for the specific 18-to-24-month Western pass-rate finding that the paper attempts to replicate across cultures and cited in the Method section as one of the Western child studies using the simplified nonlinguistic mark-test procedure adopted here. It is therefore a directly re-tested empirical benchmark rather than a method-only or generic background citation.

issues.old_quote: Although possible, two studies have assessed negative affect under similar circumstances and have failed to find the state by trait interaction that would suggest a mood cost for acting counterdispositionally (McNiel & Fleeson, 2006; McNiel et al., 2010). On the other hand, one of these samples was small (n⫽45) and both employed a within-subject design that could promote demand or carryover effects. In fact, the studies did find significant order effects and some inconsistent trait and acting condition effects on negative affect. So although there was not a significant interaction suggesting an affective cost, the full mood consequences of acting more or less extraverted require some clarification, particularly with regard to negative affect. Therefore, our studies include between-subjects manipulations, larger sample sizes, and measures of both positive and negative affect to better assess any possible distress that might accompany counterdispositional behavior.
